newsitem.title: USA: Fund investors buy choppy US stock market on dip.
newsitem.headline: Fund investors buy choppy US stock market on dip.

text.p: Mutual fund investors have so far played the U.S. stock market correction right, moving back into aggressive growth funds on the dip but also hedging by buying international and balanced funds, officials said.

"You're not seeing what everybody has feared, and that is a wholesale bailing by mutual fund investors despite some very, very choppy market activity," said Tracey Gordon, a spokeswoman for Charles Schwab & Co.

Investors appeared unfazed by the 10 percent market correction in the days after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in two years on March 25, said Steven Norwitz, a spokesman for fund company T. Rowe Price Associates.
"We have actually seen some money flow into the technology funds in the last few days," he said. "People did not panic in the midst of the correction."
Many market observers had wondered if retail investors would cease plowing billions of dollars each month into stock funds and turn and run if the market corrected.
Vanguard Group and other fund companies had issued warnings to investors, many of whom had never experienced a major correction or a bear market, not to become over-optimistic.
"Investors seemed to handle (the correction) with a greater sense of grace than many would have anticipated," Vanguard spokesman Brian Mattes said.
Charles Schwab, which sells more than 2,000 mutual funds from a wide variety of companies, saw investors move a modest $4.5 million into aggressive growth funds so far in April, Gordon said.
In March, aggressive growth funds sold through Schwab lost about $209 million in sales as the market marched to record highs, she said.

Investors continued to seek a foreign shelter from the U.S. market volatility by buying international funds in early April, she said. And the more conservative balanced funds, which invest stocks and bonds, became more popular in recent weeks after more than a year of being out of favor, she said.
Net sales of stock mutual funds offered by Schwab totalled $168 million in the first part of this month, with $33.6 million going towards balanced funds and $91 million going into index funds.
The Investment Company Institute, an industry trade group, reported on Thursday that net sales of all U.S. stock funds slowed in March to $9.5 billion from $18.45 billion in February.
The estimated flows to stock funds in March was the lowest since the $5.75 billion inflow in July 1996, when the U.S. market also suffered heavy losses.
ICI said bond and income funds had an estimated outflow of $1 billion in March, compared with an inflow of $2.17 billion in February.
Vanguard Group, whose flagship $34 billion Index 500 Portfolio has benefitted by the growing popularity of index funds, has also seen investment sentiments shift within the last week.
"We're seeing individuals move back into equities again in the last day or two," Mattes said. "Investors are moving eagerly towards equities now then they had in the prior two weeks."
